newsitem.title: USA: "Partial birth" ban won't stop late-term abortion.
newsitem.headline: "Partial birth" ban won't stop late-term abortion.

text.p: A ban on so-called "partial birth" abortion will not stop women from ending late-term pregnancies, but could spur efforts to bar other procedures and spark legal challenges from abortion rights groups.

"In terms of late-term abortion after the 20th week (of pregnancy), there are alternative late-term procedures that are accepted and taught ... other procedures that will be available," said Gene Tarne, a spokesman for Physicians Ad hoc Coalition for Truth (PHACT).

PHACT wants to ban the procedure known to opponents as "partial birth" abortion -- also known as intact dilation and extraction -- in which a foetus is partially removed from the uterus feet-first, the foetal brain is suctioned out and then the rest of the foetus is removed.

A proposed ban on the procedure passed the U.S. House of Representatives by a veto-proof margin this year and was being debated in the Senate Tuesday, with the potential to pass there by a similarly veto-proof two-thirds majority.

President Bill Clinton has vowed to veto it, saying that in addition to the present exception for cases where a woman's life is endangered, there should also be an exception for when a woman's health is in jeopardy.
The debate has been driven in part by anti-abortion forces who have graphically depicted the method in line drawings that have become fixtures in the houses of Congress.
But other legal late-term abortion procedures could be left in place by this legislation. These alternative procedures may include:
-- Dilation and evacuation, the most common abortion procedure for second trimester pregnancies, in which the foetus is dismembered inside the uterus before being extracted;
-- Induction, in which medications are used to induce labour and the foetus is expelled;
-- Hysterotomy, or pre-term Cesarean section, in which the woman's abdomen is surgically opened and the foetus removed.
Kathryn Kolbert of the Centre for Reproductive Law and Policy, said it was unclear whether the proposed ban would include limits on dilation and evacuation, or exactly what impact the ban would have.
But Kolbert said in a telephone interview that her group, which favours abortion rights, would be prepared to mount a legal challenge if the measure becomes law.

She also said that outside the legal realm, the ban would probably drive down the number of medical schools that teach the procedure, which she said was introduced as the safest method for some women, and decrease "any kind of experimentation or efforts to make abortion safer."
Kolbert also was concerned that the ban on one abortion method would pave the way for abortion opponents to seek to ban other methods.

Abortion opponents, notably the National Right to Life Committee, have focused on what they call "partial birth" abortion as a barbaric method that has no medical utility, while maintaining its position that abortion should not be allowed.

But abortion rights advocates, including the National Abortion and Reproductive Rights League, contend the constitutional rights and health of women have been jettisoned in the debate over this one procedure.
